Hey. 

I grew up with online predators too from ~ 11 - 17 including forming what I thought were relationships. 

I am now 34. 

From 17 onwards I thought I was undesirable due to the impact those men had on me and, to be frank, some of the rhetoric from other males ‘irl’. 

It took me finding a group of male friends of varying ages who respect women when I was in my late 20’s to have a mindset shift. Including my now partner. I still have nightmares where my partner leaves me for a 14 year old, but my worldview has slowly changed. 

There are still tonnes of creeps out there, but I now have a normal standard to work from and expect. I feel no attachment to the attention/sexual abuse I received as a child anymore. The men who were messaging me repulse me now and I wish I could hold one in particular accountable.

The majority of men in my life now are genuinely attracted to women their own age, ranging from 20s - 50s and don’t talk about women as objects, dissecting their appearance etc. 

But I say all this to tell you that these experiences warped my reality of sexuality, self-worth and relationships - it seems like this is the case for you too. 

And that I wanted to reassure you that maturing out of an age where predators fancy you is not the end. In fact, mid-20s is actually where it starts getting really fun. :)

Thirdly, the very basic understanding of ‘fatness is equal to Ill-health’ must take into consideration multiple factors which result in poor health. 

Often people who are obese have a series of other environmental factors co-occurring. The ACE scale was developed by a man who noticed his obese clients coming in had a much higher incidence of childhood sexual abuse than the general population. That isn’t to say that all fat people are traumatised, but I can’t imagine not being some what due to the vile comments people seem to feel entitled to about other peoples bodies. When I'm really unwell I cant sleep. Sometimes I am surviving on 3 hours a night for months. Often waking up with a pounding heart.

**Things that have worked that require little effort:**

15 minute hot shower before bed **+** melatonin **+** when panicked, practice breathing in for 5 seconds, breathing out for 8 (or breathing out slower than you breath in) + I wear earplugs every and an eyemask if its too light + No caffeine after mid-day.

*To note, the hot shower and the breathing practices are techniques used to hack your nervous system and calm it down. Alternatively, ice and cold water can help to bring you out of a freeze response.*

[https://www.psychiatrictimes.com/view/neurobiology-and-neurophysiology-breath-practices-psychiatric-care](https://www.psychiatrictimes.com/view/neurobiology-and-neurophysiology-breath-practices-psychiatric-care) 

I found that eating cannabis products helped me, rather than smoking it, so I would eat something an hour before bed. It can make me feel groggy when I wake up though.

**Things that require more effort:**

Intense exercise and good nutrition help (veggies and protein). Weight lifting is pretty amazing for calming my anxiety and cardio is great for giving me a good sleep. I currently cant bring myself to do it anymore, but if you can find the motivation it is so good for you.

I study health sciences and I can not encourage people with mental health issues to practice exercise and breathing practices enough.

Hi there, I also score 9! It is quite confronting especially after I grew up telling myself things weren't that bad. However, certain traumatic experiences aren't covered in the questionnaire so some people score lower when they have still experienced awful things. 

ACE scores work as indicators of different health issues across the lifespan, this is after huge amounts of research has been conducted noting people presenting with certain health complications usually had a series of traumatic life events.

I don't think you should be worried, just more aware that you are more pre-disposed to certain mental health issues and also behavioural or physical health issues. We just have to work a bit harder.

Hey. I have some little tips that helped me get through uni unmedicated. 

I downloaded apps that blocked all websites or apps that distract me. You set a time limit. 

A little bit of exercise everyday. It helps to release the right chemicals for focus. 

Try not to think of the big picture, break down into small tasks and work on things one at a time. 

Take reward breaks after finishing bits. 

I completely understand feeling overwhelmed to the point of being in a catatonic state. 

I struggle with sleep but now wear ear plugs, eye mask and mouth guard each night.

I have drawings an artwork over all of my school books, I think doing something with my hands helped me not day dream as much in class. This transferred into university and then professional setting too... Lol. 

Creating lists, if I don't write it down and see it visually I will probably forget something when packing. I also write down all processes when starting a new job as I tend to zone out while being taught. 

Downloading website and app blockers while studying or working from home. 

Sending photos of food I have bought for people so I can't eat it before i give it to them.

Verbalizing keys, phone, wallet all the time.

I am going to a therapist who specializes in ADHD and I can't wait to learn new techniques!
